trig-equations-basic-trigonometric-equat.title: Basic trigonometric equations
trig-equations-basic-trigonometric-equat.summary: Solve equations involving sine, cosine and tangent with special exact values; distinguish a principal inverse angle from all solutions.

blocks.text: An equation such as sin θ = a asks for every angle whose sine is a. Use the unit circle to find all angle families, not just the principal value returned by arcsin. For sine and cosine, a real solution exists only when −1 ≤ a ≤ 1.

blocks.title: Solve sin θ=1/2 for 0≤θ<2π
blocks.strategy: Use the reference angle π/6 and both positive-sine quadrants.
steps: The reference angle with sine 1/2 is π/6.
Sine is positive in quadrants I and II: θ=π/6 or θ=5π/6.
blocks.check: sin(π/6)=sin(5π/6)=1/2; no other unit-circle angles in this interval have this sine.

blocks.title: Solve cos θ=−√2/2 for 0≤θ<2π
blocks.strategy: Cosine is negative in quadrants II and III.
steps: Quadrant II gives θ=3π/4; quadrant III gives θ=5π/4.
blocks.check: Both give cosine −√2/2 and lie within the interval.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: Inverse sine alone does not list every solution of sin θ=a. Use radians unless degrees are expressly specified. Tangent has period π, whereas sine and cosine have period 2π.

blocks.prompt: Give the general solution of tan θ=1.
blocks.explanation: tan(π/4)=1; any multiple of π preserves tangent where it is defined.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial, Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§6.2–6.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §3.3; Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 14; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Chs. 10–11; Young, Trigonometry, 3rd ed., chapter on trigonometric equations. The references inform original explanations and examples.

trig-equations-general-solutions-and-spe.title: General solutions and specified intervals
trig-equations-general-solutions-and-spe.summary: Write all periodic solutions, then enumerate precisely those inside open, closed or half-open angle intervals.

blocks.text: A general solution names infinitely many coterminal or periodic angles using an integer k. A specified interval selects only the values satisfying its endpoint inequalities. Check whether 0, π or 2π are included; a half-open revolution avoids double-counting the same terminal direction.

blocks.title: Solve sin θ=0 on [0,2π)
blocks.strategy: List the integer multiples of π within the stated bounds.
steps: The general solution is θ=kπ for k∈ℤ.
From 0≤kπ<2π we get k=0 or k=1.
The solution set is {0,π}; 2π is excluded.
blocks.check: Sine is zero at 0 and π, and 2π is outside the half-open interval.

blocks.title: Solve cos θ=1/2 on (−π,π]
blocks.strategy: Use signed solutions ±π/3 and test the endpoints.
blocks.check: Both angles have cosine 1/2 and satisfy −π<θ≤π.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: A bracket [ includes an endpoint while a parenthesis ( excludes it. If an interval covers more than one revolution, count every distinct numerical angle in the interval.

blocks.prompt: How many solutions of sin θ=0 lie in [0,2π]?
blocks.explanation: Both endpoints are included, so k=0,1,2 are allowed.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial, Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§6.2–6.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §3.3; Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 14; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Chs. 10–11; Young, Trigonometry, 3rd ed., chapter on trigonometric equations. The references inform original explanations and examples.

trig-equations-equations-solved-by-facto.title: Equations solved by factoring
trig-equations-equations-solved-by-facto.summary: Factor trigonometric equations into products and solve every factor separately, preserving the original domain.

blocks.text: Treat a trigonometric function temporarily like an algebraic variable: first bring all terms to one side, factor, and apply the zero-product rule. A product is zero when at least one factor is zero. Never divide by a potentially zero factor without checking its zero case.

blocks.title: Solve sin θ(2sin θ−1)=0 on [0,2π)
blocks.strategy: Apply the zero-product rule to both factors.
steps: sin θ=0 gives θ=0 or π in the interval.
blocks.check: Every listed angle satisfies one of the original factors; the four angles are distinct.

blocks.title: Solve tan θ(tan θ−1)=0 on [0,2π)
blocks.strategy: Solve each tangent equation and check where tangent is defined.
blocks.check: At all four solutions cos θ≠0, so tan θ is defined.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: Dividing sin θ(2sin θ−1)=0 by sin θ would discard all angles with sin θ=0. Original denominators or undefined trig functions remain excluded.

blocks.explanation: sin θ=0 at 0 and π, while sin θ=−1 at 3π/2.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial, Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§6.2–6.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §3.3; Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 14; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Chs. 10–11; Young, Trigonometry, 3rd ed., chapter on trigonometric equations. The references inform original explanations and examples.

trig-equations-quadratic-type-equations.title: Quadratic-type equations
trig-equations-quadratic-type-equations.summary: Apply algebraic factoring or the quadratic formula to equations in a single trigonometric function, then reject function values outside their real ranges.

blocks.text: For equations quadratic in sin θ, cos θ or tan θ, put u equal to that function, solve the polynomial in u, and convert each admissible root into angles. Since −1≤sin θ,cos θ≤1, algebraic roots outside that range are impossible for real angles.

blocks.title: Solve 2sin²θ−sin θ−1=0 on [0,2π)
blocks.strategy: Factor in u=sin θ and solve both valid linear factors.
blocks.check: Substituting sin θ=1 and −1/2 into the polynomial gives zero.

blocks.title: Solve 2cos²θ−3cos θ+1=0 on [0,2π)
blocks.strategy: Factor and use the unit circle for each cosine value.
steps: cos θ=1/2 gives θ=π/3,5π/3; cos θ=1 gives θ=0.
blocks.check: Each solution is in the interval and makes a factor zero.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: If solving a sine-quadratic gives u=2, reject it because no real sine can equal 2. Do not reject tan θ=2: tangent has no magnitude bound.

blocks.prompt: How many solutions of sin²θ=1/4 lie in [0,2π)?
blocks.explanation: sin θ=±1/2 produces one solution in each quadrant.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial, Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§6.2–6.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §3.3; Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 14; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Chs. 10–11; Young, Trigonometry, 3rd ed., chapter on trigonometric equations. The references inform original explanations and examples.

trig-equations-equations-using-identitie.title: Equations using identities
trig-equations-equations-using-identitie.summary: Use Pythagorean and multiple-angle identities to rewrite a trigonometric equation into a solvable form, without losing zeros or changing the domain.

blocks.text: Identify an identity that converts multiple different trig functions into a common function or a product. An identity can simplify an equation, but all solutions must still be checked in the original. Division by sine or cosine may discard valid angles.

blocks.title: Solve 2sin θcos θ=sin θ on [0,2π)
blocks.strategy: Move terms to one side and factor without dividing by sin θ.
blocks.check: All four angles satisfy the original equation.

blocks.title: Solve 1−2sin²θ=0 on [0,2π)
steps: The equation is equivalent to cos 2θ=0.
blocks.check: Each angle has sin² θ=1/2, making 1−2sin² θ=0.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: An identity like cos 2θ=1−2sin² θ holds for all real θ, but tangent and quotient identities may require nonzero denominators. Never cancel a trig factor that might be zero.

blocks.prompt: Solve sin 2θ=0 for all real θ.
blocks.explanation: 2θ=kπ; divide by 2, keeping every integer k.

blocks.text: Reference guide: Lial, Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§6.2–6.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §3.3; Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 14; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Chs. 10–11; Young, Trigonometry, 3rd ed., chapter on trigonometric equations. The references inform original explanations and examples.

trig-equations-multiple-angle-equations.title: Multiple-angle equations
trig-equations-multiple-angle-equations.summary: Solve equations containing nθ, including changes in solution period and careful enumeration over a transformed interval.

blocks.text: For sin(nθ), cos(nθ) or tan(nθ), first solve for the whole argument u=nθ and then divide by n. If θ is restricted, transform the interval to an interval for u so that solutions are not skipped or double counted.

blocks.title: Solve sin 2θ=1 on [0,2π)
blocks.check: At each solution sin 2θ=1; there are two complete sine peaks over the transformed interval.

blocks.title: Solve cos 3θ=1 on [0,2π)
blocks.strategy: Solve for u=3θ and divide by three.
blocks.check: The next value k=3 gives θ=2π, excluded by the half-open interval.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not solve sin 2θ=1 as though it were sin θ=1. Dividing the argument by n changes the spacing of solutions; transform the interval as well.

Reference guide: Lial, Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§6.2–6.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §3.3; Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 14; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Chs. 10–11; Young, Trigonometry, 3rd ed., chapter on trigonometric equations. The references inform original explanations and examples.

trig-equations-equations-involving-inver.title: Equations involving inverse functions
trig-equations-equations-involving-inver.summary: Solve equations involving arcsin, arccos, and arctan by applying the corresponding trig function, while enforcing input and principal-value ranges.

blocks.text: An inverse trig function returns a principal angle. For arcsin x and arccos x, a real input requires −1≤x≤1. Their output ranges are [−π/2,π/2] and [0,π]. Arctan has any real input but outputs an angle strictly between −π/2 and π/2.

blocks.title: Solve arcsin(2x)=π/6
blocks.strategy: Apply sine, then verify both input and output domains.
steps: The input 2x=1/2 belongs to [−1,1]; π/6 is in the arcsin principal range.
blocks.check: Substitution checks the original equation: arcsin(2·1/4)=arcsin(1/2)=π/6.

blocks.title: Solve arctan x=π/2 over the reals
blocks.problem: Solve arctan x=π/2 over the reals
blocks.strategy: Check the arctangent range before applying tangent.
steps: The principal range of arctan is (−π/2,π/2).
π/2 is not in that open range. There is no real solution.
blocks.check: For every finite real x, arctan x is strictly below π/2.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not confuse arcsin x=π/6 with sin x=π/6: one is an inverse-function equation, the other is a periodic trig equation. Applying an inverse requires the correct principal branch.

Reference guide: Lial, Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§6.2–6.4; Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §3.3; Schaum’s Outline of Trigonometry, 4th ed., Ch. 14; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Chs. 10–11; Young, Trigonometry, 3rd ed., chapter on trigonometric equations. The references inform original explanations and examples.

trig-equations-extraneous-and-excluded-s.title: Extraneous and excluded solutions
trig-equations-extraneous-and-excluded-s.summary: Identify extraneous roots created by squaring or unsafe algebra, and exclude angles where the original expression is undefined.

blocks.text: A candidate is valid only if it satisfies the ORIGINAL equation and its original domain. Multiplication can produce extra roots, division can lose roots, and squaring can introduce sign-incompatible candidates. State exclusions before simplifying rational trig expressions.

blocks.title: Solve (sin²θ−1)/(sin θ−1)=0 on [0,2π)
blocks.strategy: Exclude zero denominators before cancelling factors.
steps: Original denominator sin θ−1≠0, so θ≠π/2.
With sin θ≠1, simplify to sin θ+1=0.
blocks.check: At 3π/2 the numerator is zero and denominator is −2, not zero.

blocks.title: Solve sin θ/sin θ=0 for real θ
blocks.problem: Solve sin θ/sin θ=0 for real θ
blocks.strategy: Keep the domain of the original quotient.
steps: If sin θ≠0, the quotient equals 1, not 0.
Where sin θ=0, the quotient is undefined.
Therefore there are no real solutions.
blocks.check: No real θ makes the original quotient equal zero.

blocks.title: Check extraneous roots after squaring √(1+sin θ)=sin θ
blocks.problem: For real θ, solve √(1+sin θ)=sin θ.
blocks.strategy: Check the sign of the original right side before and after squaring.
steps: Set u=sin θ. The original equation √(1+u)=u requires u≥0 and −1≤u≤1.
The positive root is outside the possible sine range; the negative root violates u≥0. No real θ satisfies the original equation.
blocks.check: Substitution into the original equation rejects both roots, even though they satisfy the squared equation.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint and reference guide

blocks.text: Cancelling sin θ−1 then substituting θ=π/2 would mistakenly add an undefined angle. Squaring both sides can give extraneous roots when the original sides have incompatible signs.

blocks.explanation: A real square root is never negative, so it cannot equal −1.

The references inform original explanations and examples.
